notifier logs show worker 2 of 3 repeating "lease renewal failed" about once a second and taking no new messages. Workers 1 and 3 are sending but cannot keep up with the batch.

row: api deploy d-4471 goes out. It carries migration 0193, which drops the old index on bookings (business_id, starts_at) and starts building a new composite index in the background.

api p95 latency for the availability endpoint rises from 180 ms to 1.9 s. CPU on the primary database reaches 92 %.
Alert fires: api p95 above 1.5 s for 3 minutes. The paging tool pages the on-call engineer.
Tom notes the last api deploy is 18 minutes old, and the slow queries in the api logs all read bookings by business and start time.
Incident declared (SEV-2). Mei takes incident commander. Support reports customers saying the booking page spins when they pick a date.
Tom rolls api back to the previous deploy, d-4466. The code goes back, but the dropped index does not come back with it.
Latency has not recovered seven minutes after the rollback. Tom pages Ravi, because the database now needs the owner's decision.
Ravi joins and finds the background index build at 41 %, with about 35 minutes left at its current speed.
Ravi decides not to recreate the old index by hand, because two index builds would compete for the same disk. The team waits for the build.
Support has 190 tickets so far. Mei posts a notice on status.sorrel.app that date search is slow and that bookings still go through.
The new index finishes building. p95 for the availability endpoint falls to 240 ms within two minutes.
Mei closes the incident after 15 minutes of normal latency and updates the status page.
Never drop an index in the same deploy that builds its replacement: drop the old one in a later deploy, after the new one is ready.
Run index builds on tables over 10 million rows outside 09:00 to 21:00 JST.

row: The daily refund job starts. It sends the 1,318 refunds approved the day before to stripe in batches of 50.
The job's connection to the payments database drops during batch 9. The job exits, and the scheduler starts it again from the beginning.
The second run sends batches 1 to 8 again. stripe accepts them as new refunds, because the idempotency keys are built from the run's start time.
Support receives the first message from a business: a customer was refunded twice for the same cancelled lesson.
Tom, on call, sees the support message in #inc-live and opens the refund job's logs, which show two runs starting at 10:00 and 10:07.
Money has already moved, so Tom pages Mei as the payments owner and changes nothing himself.
Mei acknowledges and pauses the refund job in the scheduler, so no third run can start.
Mei counts the duplicates from the stripe dashboard export: 400 refunds sent twice, ¥2,836,400 in total.
Ravi updates status.sorrel.app: refunds are paused while a payments problem is fixed; charges at checkout work normally.
Mei and finance decide the extra refunds stay with the customers and are written off. No customer will be charged again.
Mei changes the idempotency key to use the refund id instead of the run's start time. Ravi reviews the change and it is deployed.
The fixed job is run against a copy of the day's list in the stripe test account. No refund is sent twice.
Incident closed. Refunds resume with the next daily run, on 2023-10-25 at 10:00.
Build the refund idempotency key from the refund id, never from the run's start time.
Make the scheduler alert instead of restarting a job that moves money.
Write down in the payments runbook how to pause a job that moves money.

row: Aiko turns on a new cloudflare firewall rule to slow a scraper: requests to /book/* without a session cookie get a challenge page.
First-time visitors arriving from search results start getting the challenge page instead of the booking page. Most of them leave.
First customer report through support: a physiotherapy clinic says new patients cannot open its booking page.

After a second report, Tom, on call, checks the "Sorrel / web" board: booking starts from new visitors are 62 % below the same hour last week. No alert has fired, because errors and latency are normal.
Tom checks the deploy tool. The last web deploy is 2 days old, so a rollback would not help.
Tom finds 14,950 challenges on /book/* in the cloudflare firewall events since 16:02, against about 300 on a normal afternoon.
Firewall rules are never changed without Aiko, so Tom pages her with the firewall events and the booking-start panel.
Aiko acknowledges, recognises her rule from 16:02, and switches it to log only.
Challenges on /book/* fall back to normal. Booking starts from new visitors recover within ten minutes.
Mei posts on status.sorrel.app that some new visitors could not open booking pages between 16:02 and 16:58.
Aiko rewrites the rule to match only the scraper's user agent and address range, and leaves it in log-only mode for a day.
Incident closed. About 2,300 booking starts were lost in the 56 minutes the rule was active.
Alert when booking starts from new visitors fall more than 40 % below the same hour last week.
Run every new firewall rule in log-only mode for 24 hours before it blocks or challenges anything.

Tom finds 14,950 challenges on /book/* in the cloudflare firewall events since 16:02, against about 300 on a normal afternoon.

Mei posts on status.sorrel.app that some new visitors could not open booking pages between 16:02 and 16:58.
Aiko rewrites the rule to match only the scraper's user agent and address range, and leaves it in log-only mode for a day.
